output.content:
The street was not there.

That was the first thing I noticed, and the second, before I could steady the theodolite, was that I had sworn it was there when I left the office that morning.

My name is Meera Chatterjee, and I am a draughtsman for the Survey of India, which means I do not draw maps from imagination. I draw them from measurement. From angles taken in the heat and the dust and the stink of the Hooghly at low tide. From chains laid across mud. From bearings that must be true because a railway line or a telegraph pole or a widow’s hovel will be built upon them. If a street is not there, it is an error. And I, after three years in the Bengal Survey Office on Chowringhee, do not make errors.

I had been working on Ward No. 7 of Burrabazar. The men of the chain gang called it the belly, because of the meat shops and the press of bodies and the smell that never left your shirt. It was the kind of quarter that official maps simplified into clean parallel lines. I was there to make it clean.

On the 14th of November, 1896, I finished the ink work for the stretch between Chitpore Road and the lanes behind the Marwari warehouses. The sheet was dry by lamplight. I had drawn the narrow, crooked lane the Bengali clerks called *Potol Bazar* and the English clerks called Fruit Lane, a ribbon of houses no wider than a carriage, with the tea stalls on its left and the betel shops on its right. At the very end of it, tucked between a brick godown and a mosque with a green cupola, I had inked a short side street: *Sangit Lane*.

It was a mistake to name it at all. Names are not my department. But the men who chain-measured it told me the shopkeepers there called it that, after the musicians who lived in the lanes behind the Jorasanko Thakur Bari. The lane ran north-south, thirty-two paces long, and ended in a dead wall where the new tramway company had planned to cut through. I had measured it twice.

I took the sheaf of proofs home in my basket, under my sari, because the office boy was late for the tram and I did not want it to rain on the paper. My lodgings were in a second-floor room above a sweetmeat shop on College Street, with a window that looked out over the college quadrangle and in, in the mornings, the smell of jilapi.

That night, I woke at three in the morning to the sound of a street vendor moving his cart below. Kolkata never truly sleeps, but it changes its pitch. My landlady’s cat was yowling. My stomach was sour from tea. I sat up and found my map lying on the floor where I had set it to dry. I picked it up.

Sangit Lane was not where I had drawn it.

It had shifted.

Not smudged. Not a slip of ink. The lane itself had slid a hand’s breadth to the east, so that the wall at its end now overlapped the brick godown I had measured, and the little mosque with the green cupola was now half a lane too far west, its minaret overlapping the roof of a shop that had been, the night before, two doorways away.

My first thought was that I was feverish. I pressed my palms to my eyes, counted to ten, looked again. The paper was mine. The line work was mine. The hatch marks for the buildings were mine. But the relative positions had changed.

I lit the lamp. The flame made the ink swim. I fetched my brass scale, measured with a ruler. The distance between Chitpore Road and the dead wall at the end of Sangit Lane was now eight inches on the paper instead of seven and a half. On my copy, made yesterday, it was seven and a half. I checked the chain notes in my field book. The measurement was thirty-two paces. The paper said otherwise.

I laughed, a short, foolish sound. I had been up until midnight ruling. Perhaps I had redrawn it in my sleep.

Then I went to the window.

From my room I could see the lights of College Street and, beyond, the low haze over Burrabazar. It was not enough to see Potol Bazar, but I could smell it. The air had that particular wet-earth and onion smell that rose after midnight when the vendors washed their stalls. And I could hear, faintly, music.

A sarangi, thin and mournful, playing in the distance. The sound came from north, from the direction of Burrabazar.

I dressed. The night was warm. I wrapped my sari tightly and took my map in my basket, and my small compass, and slipped down the stairs. The sweetmeat shop was dark. The street was lit by the flickering gas lamps that the Municipality had installed on College Street and left out here to the shopkeepers.

There were men playing cards under a lamppost. One of them looked up.

“Miss Chatterjee?” he said. “So late?”

“Rahim,” I said. That was the boy who ran errands for my landlady.

“Ma will be angry,” he said.

“Tell her I had to check a line,” I said, which was true enough. “Do you know if the lane behind the Jorasanko house is open at this hour?”

He frowned. “Which lane?”

“Sangit Lane. Off Potol Bazar.”

He shook his head. “That lane is closed after namaz. The gatekeeper shuts it.”

I knew that. I had measured the gate. It was three feet high, wooden, always left ajar during the day.

“Tell me your way,” I said. “I’ll find it myself if I must.”

He pointed, already regretting the trouble. He’d get no tip.

I walked.

Kolkata at night is a different city. The tram tracks are empty. The dogs own the middle of the road. The smell of the Ganges drifts in low. I walked past the British Museum, past the bookstalls where the college boys would be arguing the next day, past the printing presses coughing ink into the air. The closer I got to Burrabazar, the thicker the crowd, the louder the commerce.

At last I turned onto Chitpore Road. The lane I wanted was a left turn past the marigold sellers. I found Potol Bazar easily; it was lit by sputtering oil lamps, men shouting prices for pomegranates. I could see the tea stalls on the left as on my map.

And there was the entrance to Sangit Lane.

It was not where the map said it would be.

My map placed the entrance three shops down from the tea stall with the blue awning. The entrance was now four shops down. The signboard for *Laxmi Hotel* that I had inked at the mouth of the lane now sat directly above it, where a betel shop should have been. The betel shop had moved with it.

I stood in the mud. The sarangi had stopped.

A man came out of the lane with a crate on his head. He was a musician, I thought, by his kurta and the rosary on his wrist. He saw me and stopped.

“There is no lane here,” he said, not unkindly. “You are lost, memsahib.”

“There is,” I said, holding up my paper. “Sangit Lane. Thirty-two paces.”

He looked at the paper, then at the street. He smiled the way people smile at feverish Europeans. “That lane is this way.” He pointed to the right, to a narrow alley that was not on my map at all. It was choked with laundry lines and garbage, barely a foot wide between two houses.

I walked in.

The alley was dark. The compass in my hand spun once, then settled north. The sarangi was here, clearer. It came from deeper in, where the air smelled of sandalwood and wet stone.

I counted my paces. One, two, three. The alley should have been seven paces long and then opened onto a small courtyard with the green cupola. Instead it kept going. The houses on either side were the ones from my map, but in the wrong order. The shop that sold brass bells was now next to the shop that sold cloth, and the cloth shop’s sign had the bells shop’s script.

I reached the end.

Where my map said there should be a dead wall and a plan for a tramway cutting, there was instead an open street. A real street, paved with old bricks, with a line of small shops, each lit by a single lamp, each with a door open to the night. The sarangi was coming from the third shop on the left.

People moved in this street. A woman in a red sari was bargaining for fish with a vendor. A boy was carrying a bucket of water. A man with a parrot on his shoulder was reading a newspaper. None of them looked surprised to see me.

One of them did.

An old man sat on a wooden stool outside a shop that sold nothing I could name—small wooden flutes, maybe, and incense. He had white hair and a map of his own spread across his knees. It was yellowed and large. He looked at me, and then at the basket on my arm, and then at my map.

“You measure too much,” he said in Bengali, his voice soft. “The city does not like to be measured.”

“I am a Survey officer,” I said. “The city belongs to the government.”

He laughed, a dry sound. “The government belongs to the city.” He tapped the paper on his knees. “Last night you moved Sangit Lane. The night before that you moved the lane behind the mosque in Bow Bazar. You always draw it first. Then it goes.”

“I didn’t move it,” I said, and my voice sounded thin. “It moved.”

“Yes,” he said. “It moves when you look away. That is the way it is. The street is a shy thing. Or a restless thing. It does not wish to be fixed.”

Behind him, the sarangi player lifted his bow. The note he drew was low and sorrowful.

I realized my map was no longer in my basket. I had set it on the ground when I arrived, and now it lay open on the bricks. The ink of Sangit Lane had bled, the line shifting even as I watched, sliding east again, the mosque cupola overlapping the godown, the dead wall creeping toward the tramway plan.

I bent to pick it up. The old man placed his hand over mine.

“Do not correct it,” he said. “If you correct it, it will move again. If you leave it as it is, it will stay.”

“Where are we?” I asked.

He smiled. “We are in the street you were trying to make. You are supposed to have finished the map by now, Meera Chatterjee. And when the map is finished, the city is finished.”

The sarangi stopped. The woman with the fish called out to me in a language I did not know.

I looked down at my field book, which I had not opened. The page for the 14th of November was blank.

The street behind me was closing.

I could see the bricks of the dead wall sliding back into place, the lamp lights dimming, the people stepping back as if into mist. The old man’s shop was gone, replaced by the blank brick I had measured at noon. The sarangi was a memory.

Then the man with the parrot turned his head and looked straight at me.

“You have to choose,” he said, and his voice was no longer his own. It was the voice of the city itself, low and many-mouthed. “Will you map us, or will you let us map you?”

The lane was nearly gone.

I opened my mouth to answer, and the street swallowed the sound.
